title: Nodding Syndrome: Nursing Leadership and Health Policy Amid Aetiological Uncertainty—A Structured Narrative Review
content: Background/Objectives: Nodding syndrome is a disabling neurological condition affecting communities in East Africa. Although its aetiology remains uncertain, affected individuals and families have substantial care needs. This review examined evidence relevant to nursing leadership, service coordination and health policy. Methods: We conducted a structured narrative synthesis of 31 reports directly addressing nodding syndrome and six contextual reports, identified through four bibliographic databases and supplementary sources up to 30 September 2026. Design-specific Joanna Briggs Institute critical appraisal informed interpretation using Walt and Gilson’s health policy triangle. This was not a formal systematic review. Results: The literature documents needs in seizure management, continuity of antiseizure medicines, rehabilitation, follow-up, caregiver support, stigma reduction and community trust. Barriers include medicine shortages, transport costs, fragmented referrals and resource constraints. Nursing activities recur across education, surveillance, follow-up and coordination, but studies rarely isolate the effects of nurse-led care. Evidence for nodding-syndrome-specific prevention remains insufficient. Conclusions: Aetiological uncertainty does not remove the responsibility to organize essential care. Nursing coordination and community participation are evidence-informed proposals for addressing documented service gaps, but their clinical effectiveness, feasibility, equity and sustainability require prospective evaluation. Proposed service models should not be presented as proven interventions or as preventing nodding syndrome.
